comparison: Both evaluate receptive field spatial reorganization claims (C4, C35-C38). OpenEval finds the statistical analyses appropriate and the correlation results significant. Peer reviewers question the relevance and note 'no statistics provided' for Figure 4C, requesting either statistical tests, more data, or removal of this section.

Both address the sub-to-suprathreshold transition (C46-C48, C21-C23, C27-C29). OpenEval finds the link between small voltage changes and large spiking changes well-supported by statistical results. Peer reviewers find 'it is difficult to reconcile these two findings' and question whether the authors make a convincing case, requesting additional analysis and modeling to explain how 20% EPSP changes produce 200% spike probability changes.

Both evaluate the computational model explaining in vivo vs in vitro STDP timing discrepancies (C5, C39-C45, C59-C64). Both find the modeling results acceptable. OpenEval emphasizes the model's coherence and testable predictions. Peer reviewers do not challenge the jitter-based explanation, though they request additional modeling for other aspects of the data.

Both address positive timing protocol results (C2, C21-C23, C26, C33, C51). OpenEval finds converging experimental evidence with appropriate statistical tests. Peer reviewers express concern about measurement reliability, noting figures suggest 'sometimes only a single spike response' and requesting more detailed statistics to support baseline estimates.

Both evaluate negative timing (LTD) protocol results (C3, C24-C25). OpenEval finds the bidirectional timing-dependent effects appropriately demonstrated. Peer reviewers note 'a surprising finding' that LTD affects subthreshold but not spiking output, suggesting 'the data look more like a negative control' and requesting clearer discussion of why experiments may be inconclusive.

Both address control experiments (C30-C31). OpenEval finds control experiments appropriately rule out confounds. Peer reviewers note the sham control 'could be because the STDP protocol does change something, but maybe not what the authors propose' and state 'No negative control experiments are provided...regarding subthreshold activity,' questioning whether effects depend on spike pairing or just depolarization.

Both evaluate broader conclusions about STDP function (C6-C7, C34, C53-C54, C65-C66, C69). OpenEval finds interpretations well-supported and appropriately contextualized. Peer reviewers fundamentally question whether STDP specifically underlies the effects, stating 'Certainly the results are consistent with STDP, but they do not demonstrate definitively that STDP definitively underlies the plasticity' and noting alternative mechanisms should be discussed.

Both address STDP mechanism interpretation (C1, C40-C41, C43). OpenEval finds the computational model provides mechanistic insight. Peer reviewers challenge the STDP-specific interpretation, noting 'the authors have pushed very strongly the idea that STDP in particular (as opposed to classical Hebbian LTP/LTD) underlies the phenomenology' and requesting acknowledgment of alternative possibilities like changes in inhibition or intrinsic conductances.

OpenEval evaluates methodological details and basic observations (C56-C58, C20) as clearly documented and appropriate. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these specific methodological claims.
OpenEval evaluates background context and literature citations (C8-C19, C68) as appropriate and well-supported. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these background claims.

OpenEval finds theoretical interpretations and general principles (C69-C76) extend beyond direct experimental evidence and require additional validation. While peer reviewers question related interpretive claims in R8, the specific theoretical framing claims in OpenEval R8 are not directly addressed in peer reviews.
